Niacin and pellagra
325


Absorption, Transport, and Storage
Preformed niacin (formerly vitamin B3) occurs in foods either as nicotinamide (niacinamide) or as the pyridine (i.e., nicotinamide)
nucleotide coenzymes derived from it, or as nicotinic acid, which lacks the amide nitrogen, and is the form known as niacin in North
America. Both nicotinamide and nicotinic acid are equally effective in vitamin potency, but in large doses, they exert markedly
different pharmacological effects; thus, it is important, at least in that context, to make the distinction.
The most important sources of preformed niacin in most foods, particularly animal foods, are the pyridine (i.e., nicotinamide)
nucleotides, NAD(H) and NADP(H). Hydrolases and pyrophosphatases in biological tissues convert these coenzymes to tissue
sources of the vitamin. NAD glycohydrolase and pyrophosphatase enzymes are present in the gut mucosa, and absorption of nico-
